data.title: Middle East Eye: ‘We do not want to die from the cold’: Gaza families struggle as rain floods shelters
data.author: Katherine Hearst
data.summary:
‘We do not want to die from the cold’: Gaza families struggle as rain floods shelters
Mansour al-Sakni, 33, watched helplessly as rainwater flooded the makeshift shelter on the roof of a building in Gaza City's al-Tuffah neighbourhood, where he lives with his wife and four children.
The family had replaced their old tarpaulins with new ones just two weeks ago. Sakni had sold two water barrels so they could buy new sheets to keep them dry and sheltered.
But when the first winter storm swept across the Gaza Strip, the canopy offered little protection.
“We woke up and found ourselves surrounded by water. The children were crying. I did not know what to do, and I started crying too,” Sakni told Middle East Eye.
“We stood inside the tarpaulin shelter waiting for the rain to stop so we could try to push the water out of the room.”

data.title: Middle East Eye: US midterms: Not even Trump's Israel aid stunt could rescue the Republicans
data.author: Mohamad Elmasry
data.summary:
US midterms: Not even Trump's Israel aid stunt could rescue the Republicans
Submitted by
Mohamad Elmasry
on
Thu, 11/05/2026 - 18:21
Washington's support for its ally has become an electoral liability, but ending the annual funding package could pave the way for deeper military cooperation
A Democratic campaign sign showing a mugshot of US President Donald Trump lies on the ground outside a polling station in Indianapolis during the midterm election, on 3 November (USA Today Network via Reuters)
Off
There is nothing particularly unusual about an election stunt. Politicians routinely perform them. Rarely, though, is a stunt as obvious as the one US President Donald Trump pulled on 3 November, Election Day, when he announced that America would, at year's end, stop providing $4bn in annual military aid to Israel.
Trump had clearly read the room, and the polls.
For all his public disdain for polls he claims are "fake" or "rigged", the president understands their political significance.
Polling data suggests that American voters are increasingly uncomfortable contributing their tax dollars to Israel's military, particularly as costs rise in the US and Americans struggle to afford basic necessities.
An August Marquette Law School poll, for example, found that 52 percent of American adults believe Washington provides Israel with too much military aid. Only 16 percent said it provides too little. Even among Republicans under 30, 54 percent said Washington gives Israel too much.
Appearing on Fox & Friends that morning, Trump asked why Republicans should "suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed", a reference to Abdul El-Sayed, who hours later would become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. Funding for Israel, Trump said, had become "a bad talking point" for Republicans.
The admission was remarkable, and it demonstrated, perhaps more clearly than anything else, the extent to which a mainstay of American foreign policy has turned into an electoral liability.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards has said that it has lifted restrictions on the range of Iran's missiles.
IRGC spokesman, Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi reportedly made the comments at a press conference on Saturday, in response to question regarding the country's supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei's warning to the US against further attacks on the country.
Khamenei had previously said during a meeting with senior military commanders, that any renewed US or Israeli attck would be met with "with an immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response".
The leader also reportedly ordered an update of Iran's military target database.
According to Tasnim news agency, Mohebbi was asked on Saturday whether Khamenei's comments meant that limits on the range of Iranian missiles had been removed. He responded : "This restriction has been lifted for us".
“Our duty is to show our capabilities on the battlefield,” he added.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Palestinian Minister of Health warns of outbreak of disease in storm-battered Gaza
data.author: Katherine Hearst
data.summary:
Palestinian Minister of Health warns of outbreak of disease in storm-battered Gaza
Palestinian Health Minister Majed Abu Ramadan has warned of the risk of the outbreak of disease in Gaza as tens of thousands of displaced people have faced flooding while sheltering in makeshift tents.
Israeli restrictions have meant scarce aid- and in particular, shelter materials- is entering the strip, leaving almost all of Gaza's population exposed to the elements and health risks amid rapidly deteriorating sanitation conditions.
Abu Ramdan emphasised that the razing of infrastructure by Israel as part of its onslaught on Gaza has amplified the health risks. Overcrowded displacement camps and the cold and damp conditions inside damaged tents could expose children, infants and elderly people to an elevated risk of respiratory infections.
Meanwhile, lack of clean water, busted sewage systems, and mounting waste pose the risk of water and food contamination, as well as the spread of rodents and insects.
Abu Ramadan also emphasised that widespread malnutrition, particularly among children and pregnant women, means their bodies will be less able to fight off infections.
"What is happening in Gaza is not a passing winter crisis, but an escalating threat to public health and people's lives that requires immediate international action commensurate with the scale of the catastrophe," Abu Ramadan said.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Saudi-led strikes kill at least 27 in Yemen's Sanaa, Houthis say
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Saudi-led strikes kill at least 27 in Yemen's Sanaa, Houthis say
Saudi-led coalition air strikes killed 27 people, most of them women and children, in Yemen’s Sanaa province, the Houthis said on Saturday.
The Houthi-run health ministry told the group’s Saba news agency that 36 people were also wounded in the strikes on the village of Al-Shariya.
Saba reported earlier on Saturday that rescuers were still recovering victims from the rubble, and that warplanes had struck paramedics twice.
The Houthis, meanwhile, said they had carried out six missile and drone operations against Saudi targets in the kingdom and inside Yemen, including Aramco oil facilities, Riyadh airport, and Saudi troops and military positions on both sides of the border.
The Saudi-led coalition said on Saturday it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi missile fired towards Riyadh province.
Separately, Yemeni government forces announced that they had struck 875 Houthi sites and gatherings in the past few hours as part of an offensive they call Operation Dawn of Yemen, which they say aims to retake Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa.
On Friday, an attack on a market in Taiz province killed 30 people. The Houthis blamed Saudi air strikes, while government forces accused the group of firing a ballistic missile at the site.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Israel's president picks Eisenkot over Netanyahu to try to form new government
data.author: MEE staff
data.summary:
Israel's president picks Eisenkot over Netanyahu to try to form new government
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Sat, 11/07/2026 - 19:52
Former army chief, backed by both Arab-led parties, has 28 days to build a coalition as Netanyahu fights to stay in power
Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, waves following national election exit polls at his party headquarters in Tel Aviv, Israel, 28 October 2026 (REUTERS/Shir Torem)
Off
Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Saturday chose opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to try to form a new government, Israeli media reported, after an inconclusive election left neither he nor Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu with a clear path to power.
Eisenkot, a former military chief, is due to formally receive the mandate on Sunday evening.
He will then have 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension.
Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc won 53 seats in the 27 October election, short of the 61 needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, though it remains the largest grouping in parliament.
The opposition alliance led by Eisenkot won 48, while Arab-led parties secured a record 19 seats between them, giving them a potentially decisive role in coalition talks.
Both Arab-led parties backed Eisenkot during consultations with Herzog this week.
Ra’am, led by Mansour Abbas, endorsed him with its eight lawmakers on Wednesday, followed by the Joint List on Thursday.
That brought Eisenkot’s total to 67 lawmakers, against 46 for Netanyahu.
United Torah Judaism, which had backed Netanyahu after the previous five elections, declined to recommend him this time, though it did not back Eisenkot either.
The Joint List said its unanimous decision reflected public demand to stop Netanyahu and his government from returning to power, and was aimed at widening Eisenkot’s lead to improve the chances of replacing the incumbent government.
After the consultations, Herzog said on Thursday it would be logical to give the mandate to Eisenk

data.title: Middle East Eye: Iraq has evidence outside parties use its territory to attack neighbours: Foreign minister
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Iraq has evidence outside parties use its territory to attack neighbours: Foreign minister
Iraq has evidence that external parties have been using its territory to attack neighbouring countries, Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said in an interview with Al Jazeera on Saturday.
Hussein said Baghdad was investigating attacks launched from Iraqi soil against Gulf states and wanted to resolve its differences with Saudi Arabia "through frank dialogue".
Riyadh has accused Iran-aligned groups in Iraq of targeting its oil infrastructure. In September, Baghdad confirmed that the drones that struck the kingdom’s East-West pipeline had been launched from Iraqi territory.
Last month, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi assured Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman that Iraq would not be used as a launchpad for attacks on the kingdom.
During the interview, Hussein said Baghdad was negotiating with Iran-aligned factions to bring their weapons under state control, a process he said must rely on dialogue, not force.
He added that Iraq had told Tehran it welcomed friendship and an alliance but rejected interference in its internal affairs.
Iraq lost about $60bn while oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz were suspended following the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, Hussein said.

US military says it disabled cargo vessel in Gulf of Oman
A US military aircraft fired on and disabled a commercial vessel that tried to break the US naval blockade of Iran on Saturday, US Central Command (Centcom) said.
The St Kitts and Nevis-flagged cargo ship had visited an Iranian port and was trying to leave regional waters when a US plane fired precision munitions at its stern, after US forces ordered the crew to clear the targeted areas of the vessel, Centcom said.
The US military also said on Saturday it was launching a task force to crack down on Iran’s movement of advanced weapons and other sanctioned material across its land borders and through the Caspian Sea, expanding on its months-long naval blockade.
Centcom estimated that the blockade had prevented Iran from exporting more than $25bn worth of crude oil.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Iran's army says forces 'stronger' than at start of war, Hormuz to stay closed
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Iran's army says forces 'stronger' than at start of war, Hormuz to stay closed
Iran's armed forces are "on higher alert and are stronger than they were at the beginning of the war" with the United States, an army spokesman said on Saturday.
"They now possess greater motivation, commitment and self-confidence," Mohammad Akraminia told the official IRNA news agency, adding that the Strait of Hormuz would stay closed until Washington met Tehran's demands.
"Under the order of the Supreme Leader, the response of the armed forces will be immediate, effective and without geographical limitations," he said.
Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesman Hossein Mohebbi told the Fars news agency that "the increase in the range of Iran's missiles continues steadily".
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Instagram that he had held calls with counterparts from 12 countries over the past 48 hours, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Turkey, Egypt, Iraq and Pakistan.
He said he had stressed "the legitimate right of our country to defend its sovereignty and national security" and called for "regional security arrangements without the interference of superregional powers".
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump called Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani on Friday to discuss efforts to end the war.
On Friday, the US military offered a $20m reward "and possible relocation" for information on Iran's nuclear programme.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Israeli military issues orders to seize Palestinian land and uproot trees near Bethlehem
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Israeli military issues orders to seize Palestinian land and uproot trees near Bethlehem
Israeli authorities have issued four military orders to seize Palestinian land near Bethlehem in the occupied West Bank, including orders to seize 4.708 dunums of land in al-Khader and Arab al-Ta'amra and remove trees and vegetation from 10.085 dunums in Nahalin, the Palestinian Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission said.
The orders, issued on 28 October, place routes and sites under direct military control and require the removal of trees and vegetation around the settlements.
One order covers a route cutting through agricultural terraces, linked to a plan to build a tower. The commission said its impact would extend well beyond the seized land.
It also documented 674 attacks by Israeli forces and settlers on Palestinian farmers and olive trees across the West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, between 1 October and 6 November. More than three-quarters were carried out by settlers.
On Saturday, an Israeli settler assaulted a Palestinian man near Kisan, east of Bethlehem, and stole his belongings and groceries, local sources told the Palestinian news agency Wafa.
In central Hebron, settlers smashed the windows of a Palestinian home on al-Shuhada Street.
Near Anin, west of Jenin, they stopped farmers from harvesting olives next to a newly established outpost.
Israeli forces seized a tractor and harvested olives west of nearby Arraba, detaining several Palestinians picking olives on their own land.
South of Hebron, Israeli forces detained two brothers as they harvested olives east of Yatta and seized vehicles and tractors in Masafer Yatta.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Yemen and Lebanon to work towards halting Hezbollah support for Houthis, minister says
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
Yemen and Lebanon to work towards halting Hezbollah support for Houthis, minister says
Yemen's Foreign Minister Afrah al-Zouba has said her government will take joint measures with Lebanon to halt Hezbollah's support to Houthis.
In a post on X, which came after the meeting of Lebanese President Joseph Aoun and Yemen's Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, al-Zouba said her government appreciated Lebanon's support for Yemen’s sovereignty, unity, and territorial integrity, and "rejection of any military intervention in its internal affairs".
"We affirm the importance of building on this position through coordination between the relevant authorities in our two countries to follow up on our government’s announcement regarding the role of Hezbollah members in supporting the military operations of the terrorist Houthi militia," she wrote.
"We reaffirm Yemen’s support for Lebanon’s sovereignty, security, and stability, and for the Lebanese state’s efforts to extend its authority over its entire territory and to retain exclusive control over weapons and decisions of war and peace," al-Zouba added.
نثمّن عالياً موقف لبنان الشقيق، قيادةً وحكومةً، الداعم لسيادة اليمن ووحدته وسلامة أراضيه، والرافض لأي تدخل عسكري في شؤونه الداخلية. ونؤكد أهمية البناء على هذا الموقف عبر التنسيق بين الجهات المختصة في بلدينا لمتابعة ما أعلنته حكومتنا بشأن دور عناصر من حزب الله في دعم العمليات العسكرية لمليشيا الحوثي الإرهابية، واتخاذ إجراءات مشتركة لوقف هذا الدعم ومنع تجدّده. ونجدد دعم اليمن لسيادة لبنان وأمنه واستقراره، ولجهود الدولة اللبنانية الرامية إلى بسط سلطتها على كامل أراضيها، وحصر السلاح وقرار الحرب والسلم بيدها. كما نؤكد حرصنا على تعزيز العلاقات الأخوية بين بلدينا على أساس الاحترام المتبادل وبما يخدم المصالح المشتركة.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Death toll from air strikes near Yemeni capital rises to 33, Houthis say
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Death toll from air strikes near Yemeni capital rises to 33, Houthis say
The death toll from Saturday's air strikes on a village near Yemen's capital, Sanaa, has risen to at least 33, with 39 wounded, Houthis said, in one of the deadliest reported attacks since fighting between Saudi Arabia and the group resumed in July.
The Houthis' Saba news agency said the strikes were carried out by Saudi Arabia. Riyadh has not claimed the attack.
The Houthi-run health ministry said the strikes hit homes in the Bani Hushaysh area, a Houthi stronghold east of Sanaa, and that most of those killed were women and children.
Abdul-Aziz al-Dailami, director of Sehatuna Hospital in Sanaa, said many victims remained trapped under the rubble, including first responders.
"The strikes keep coming. Just as rescuers arrive, another strike hits. We have even lost some of our own medical responders, who have been martyred," he told Reuters.
"We received a number of wounded individuals in very critical condition, with injuries to the head, chest and legs, as well as fractures," al-Dailami added.
A Yemeni man carries a wounded child into a hospital after an air strike on a village in the Bani Hushaysh district, located on the eastern outskirts of Sanaa, 7 November 2026 (Mohammed HUWAIS / AFP)
